newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: FOCUS-East European shares mixed in summer lull.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-East European shares mixed in summer lull.

text.p: Central and east European bourses had mixed fortunes this week with Warsaw and Romania leading the gainers and Prague shrugging off a government confidence vote to close moderately higher.

Budapest ended a run of spectacular gains with a widely predicted correction in mid-week and Bratisalva continued to fall sharply. Ljubliana saw moderate losses and Croatian shares picked up, though analysts forecast price stagnation in both markets with few fresh factors seen.
The Central European Share Index (CESI), which measures price movements in 72 Czech, Hungarian, Polish, Slovak and Slovenian shares, moved higher.
PRAGUE
Czech shares edged slightly higher in a week dominated by a parliamentary confidence vote in the centre-right coalition government which, to the relief of many investors, the government won.

As tension surrounding the vote receded, dealers said the market would now redirect its sights to more fundamental economic issues such as government promises to regulate the capital markets and rein in the budget deficit.
"Now it is time to get back to work and clean up the markets, stop corruption...it is the government's job to do this," said Jan Sykora of Wood and Company.
WARSAW
The Warsaw WIG index rose 3.0 percent this week, but analysts said the pace of growth was likely to slow with trading reverting back to the long term flat trend it has been on for several weeks.
Analysts said investor attention was likely to focus on the 15 National Investment Funds (NFI), of Poland's mass privatisation scheme, which started trading on the bourse on Thursday.

"The growth doesn't look like a longer-term tendency, I suspect investors will start selling soon and the market's attention will shift to NFIs," said Dariusz Szepieniec, an analyst at Bank Slaski brokerage.
Analysts said bourse sentiment was likely to remain overshadowed by the prospect of large privatisations and general elections due in September.
BUDAPEST
Hungarian shares had a rollercoaster week, that started with the seventh successive daily record high on Monday.
Traders said improving macroeconomic figures and good corporate earnings fuelled the price rises.
But a two-day correction pulled prices down sharply before recovering on Thursday when major issues nudged the BUX back up.
Traders said Hungarian shares were likely to be stable for the next few weeks, but added that the long-term outlook remains positive.
BUCHAREST

Increased foreign interest in the Bucharest bourse after the announcement of new portfolio investment rules sent turnover to consecutive all-time highs on Wednesday and Thursday and the two main indices posted strong gains towards the end of the week.
Earlier this week, Romania set a 1.5 percent tax on each portfolio buying deal, amending previous portfolio flow rules which set a four percent fee on capital gains.
BRATISLAVA

The 16-share SAX index continued to decline in light trading on the Bratisalva Stock Exchange (BSE) with brokers expecting little change until there is a resolution to the current uncertainty surrounding the Slovak crown.
"The decline is fuelled mainly by fears of a Slovak crown devaluation, but also the start of a listless summer season seems to be playing its role," said Dusan Sykora of ING Barings.
Sykora said he did not expect a reversal of the downtrend or a significant improvement in liquidity for at least two months.
"The index might not significantly fall further, but in a wider perspective, the downtrend will be still visible at least by the end of the summer," he said.
LJUBLJANA
In Slovenia, prices and volumes fell with traders predicting a quiet summer season in the absence of any fresh factors to boost the market.
Market participants said future movements would largely depend on ratification of the EU association agreement, which was signed in June last year.
ZAGREB
Most Croatian stocks closed firmer in slow trading on Friday, but dealers forecast livelier business next week though prices were not expected to move dramatically.
"I don't see any huge leaps in prices but investors are definitely interested in buying larger share packages," said Marko Nikolac of Metroholding brokerage.
